title: Experts and charlatans: The role of science in democracy
subtitle: Science and Representative Democracy
author: Mauro Dorato
introduction: With the rise of technology and often impenetrable science, societies run the risk of becoming technocratic, with a widening divide between experts and citizens. Under such conditions, for democracy to function citizens must be able to perceive the difference between real experts and charlatans. To do this, Mauro Dorato argues, we must not only increase scientific literacy, but we must also better understand the social rules at play in scientific fields, such as peer review and repeatability of proofs, in order to tell the difference between the expert and the charlatan.
body:
How specialisation can threaten democracy

Contemporary democracies are under threat. Many regard the unstoppable immigration waves as a danger to their possessions and as an occupation of their territories to be defended by erecting walls. The growing inequality and impoverishment of the middle class within democratic states can generate authoritarian drives that lead to limitations of civil rights.

However, in order the explain the current crisis of representative democracies, other serious problems must be considered, caused by the widening gap between the principle of competence necessary for rational deliberations – provided by scientists and more generally by experts – and the principle of the autonomy of choice, a fundamental right that non-omniscient citizens living in a democracy must enjoy. The prevailing misinformation and disinformation made possible by the superluminal transmission of information via social media must therefore be taken into serious consideration too.

Unlike the natural sciences, the moral sciences have not undergone a conceptual upheaval that freed them from an outdated method of inquiry.

John Dewey claimed that the survival of democracies depends on a revolution in our systems of education. According to him, the well-being of democracies is correlated with high levels of literacy, where the latter essentially hinges on the application of the empirical science’s experimental method to the most pressing social problems. Unlike the natural sciences, the moral sciences have not undergone a conceptual upheaval that freed them from an outdated method of inquiry.

Dewey’s message is still valid, but nowadays the conflict between the principle of autonomy and the principles of competence has become even more radical. In my Science and Representative Democracy (Bloomsbury 2023) I have proposed to steer a mid-course between the Scylla of populism and the Charybdis of technocracies. The advancement of science and technology depends on exponentially growing processes of specialization, accompanied by the creation of technical languages that are evermore inaccessible to the large public and even to scientists working in different fields.

The indispensable, ever increasing role of experts regarded as mediators of scientific knowledge threatens the autonomy of choice of the citizens.

Technocracy and Populism

On the one hand, technocratic regimes, which could be advocated in the name of the principle of competence, do not solve the conflict and must also be avoided, given that in this case few experts would decide for all without considering the aims of the citizens. The indispensable, ever increasing role of experts regarded as mediators of scientific knowledge threatens the autonomy of choice of the citizens. The risk in this case is a degeneration of representative democracies into technocracies, where few experts decide for all. The citizens would be deprived of their autonomy in this case, since the elected politicians would not take responsibility for their choices. Of course, they ought to rely on science, but should not justify their decisions only by bringing to bear the unassailable “intimations of science”. Examples of this attitude could be found also during the Covid 19 period.

SUGGESTED READING How modern medicine became dangerous By David Healy

Using the metaphor of German sociologist Max Weber, science is like a map. It does not tell us where we should go – an issue that depends on our aims and cannot be suggested by scientific knowledge – but only how to get in an objective way where we want to go.

On the other, specialization processes are incompatible with giving more autonomy of choice to the citizens by escaping in utopistic populistic regimes where, typically, (i) scientific illiteracy rules (ii) all scientists are regarded as a corrupt élite, (iii) the citizens’ justifiable demand of autonomous choices of social policies is illusorily compensated by frequent plebiscites. These instruments of direct democracies are important but cannot be used to decide with a ‘like’ or ‘dislike’ questions that have not been raised by the citizens, and about which they are necessarily uninformed and more subject to misinformation. The totalitarian threat raised by “hyper-participatory” democracies has been stressed by the Italian philosopher Norberto Bobbio: “individuals requested from dawn to dusk to participate to common discussions in order to exercise their political duties as citizens would be not the ‘total’ persons but the ‘total’ citizens… and the latter are the other face of the total State”.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Is specialisation killing us? With Caitjan Gainty, Nick Lane, David Healy, Mark Salter

Against these two extremes, I claim that representative democracies based on a higher level of scientific literacy are the best way to find a balance between participatory forms of citizenship and the right to devote our life to pursue our own objectives by delegating more competent fellow-citizens to suggest ways to achieve social objectives of common interest. Finding such a balance is perhaps the most urgent problem that our democracies need to confront, since it is key to begin to tackle the issues denounced in the opening paragraph. Cooperative attitudes based on empirical knowledge are the most rational and farsighted way that the human species has found during its evolution to live together by promoting at the same time the interest of each member.

Given the impossibility of omniscient citizens already recognized by Dewey, it is of paramount importance to be aware of the problem-solving, social nature of acquisition of scientific knowledge.

The realization of ideal representative democracies presupposes, however, very effective selection criteria of politicians and therefore, in western countries, a much higher level of scientific literacy.

This literacy of course cannot compensate the advance of specialization referred to above. Therefore, it is important to keep in mind that the formation of a scientific mindset presupposes a few elements that can be realistically achieved via some acquaintance with the history and philosophy of science. For instance, how are, in general, empirical hypotheses confirmed by data? How can the fallibility and the reliability of scientific beliefs coexist? What is the role of consensus in the acceptance of a scientific hypothesis?

Finding a way forward

In my book I argue that a response to these questions involves a familiarity with the social mechanics of assessment of scientific hypotheses (peer review, repeatability of proofs as well as experiments whenever possible, presentations of new theses at scientific workshops, etc.). Knowledge of these social institutions increases the probability that citizens can choose competently between real experts and swindlers and ‘merchants of doubt’ (to use Conway & Oreskes’ expression).

The methodology that needs to be adopted to increase our scientific literacy must be based on a historical-philosophical approach to the growth of science. Such an approach is important for various reasons: not only does it helps us to trace the most essential conquests of our cultural history with their de-anthropomorphizing valence. It also, more importantly, helps us to learn how, during the history of ideas, we have become capable of learning more. Learning how to learn. Given the impossibility of omniscient citizens already recognized by Dewey, it is of paramount importance to be aware of the problem-solving, social nature of acquisition of scientific knowledge. The justification of almost all our beliefs depends on our trusting the beliefs of others: the web of beliefs acquires every day an enormous number of nodes and connections among them. The validation of a new scientific hypothesis depends on a very intricate trial and error mechanism that is made possible by peer review, repeatable experiments and proofs, public workshop, and especially the logical consistency with what has been established so far. In addition, becoming aware of the historical dimension of science frees us from the myth of its absolute certainty, a form of fallibilism that, however, should be distinguished from a superficial form of relativism, which is in part responsible of the loss of credibility of science and scientists also among some intellectual quarters. Finally, knowledge of the growth science reinforces our belief in the existence of an objective, intersubjectively valid knowledge that is not exposed to the whims of economic and other partial interests: later theories generalize earlier ones, which are never jettisoned like a useless ballast.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Trust, science and neutrality With Tara Shears, Bret Weinstein, Hilary Lawson, Terence Kealey

These characteristics of science can provide many useful indications for reforming and strengthening representative democracies which, we should recall, are a very small minority in today’s political panorama. First, we should consider the relationship between science and democracy from the perspective of the values and the norms that ground them. Pluralism, with its complex relationship with values like consensus and objectivity, tolerance, respect for facts, impartiality, and openness to criticism and doubt has played and still plays an important role both in the growth of scientific knowledge and in the rules governing a democracy. On the contrary, conformism and dogmatism have been and still are obstacles to the health of both institutions. One of the reasons that explains these shared commitments to these values calls into play the growing historical awareness that, from the viewpoint of possession of rational capacities, persons are equal. The necessity to justify one’s scientific belief is mirrored by the necessity to justify in a rational way the introduction of new bills or more radical constitutional reforms.

Decisions in science and in a representative democracy ... both share a fundamental commitment to practical problem-solving, where ‘problem’ should be interpreted in the broadest possible sense.

The obvious difference between the social mechanisms leading to decisions in science and in a representative democracy are assuaged by the fact both share a fundamental commitment to practical problem-solving, where ‘problem’ should be interpreted in the broadest possible sense. Finding out the effectiveness of a vaccine is an epistemic problem that can be solved – when knowledge is sufficient – in the prudential sense entailed by statistical risks. This epistemic problem generates the much more difficult problem of finding a rational strategy on the part of the political class that, importantly, mediating between the conflicting values of the segments of the involved citizens.

SUGGESTED READING The myth of value-free science By Melanie Challenger

In conclusion, the future of democracies is essentially linked to a more just distribution of resources. The solution to this problem, however, presupposes the cognizance that the cooperation among different individuals and different groups is the best way to promote the interest of all, a claim that is confirmed by a study of our evolutionary past that should be encouraged more to understand our place on earth. Just another piece of evidence that, as Mandela put it, “education is the most powerful weapon that you can use to change the world.”

Mauro Dorato's latest book Science and Representative Democracy: Experts and Citizens was published in 2023 by Bloomsbury.
